characters.name: Goran
characters.origin_detail: the towns and neighbourhoods of Bosnia and Herzegovina
characters.voice_style: a low, dry monotone — like a man who’s survived three wars and now speaks only in proverbs, bullet points, and the occasional sigh
characters.political_temperament: believes every government is a bad joke, but the coffee shop is the only place where the joke is still funny — because everyone’s in on it
mannerisms: Serves coffee with a spoon. Says, ‘If you don’t stir it, the truth sinks.’
When asked about the war, replies: ‘We lost everything. Except our sense of humor. And that was the last thing they couldn’t take.’
Always has a single cigarette behind his ear. He never lights it. ‘For the ghosts,’ he says. ‘They like the smell.’
Answers every question with a story about someone else — and leaves you wondering if he was the one who did it.
backstory_lines: Goran once sold a man a loaf of bread during a siege — and charged him in memories.
Goran has never voted. He says, ‘I already know who’s lying. I just wait for them to forget they’re lying.’
Goran doesn’t believe in peace treaties. He believes in coffee breaks.
characters.backstory: Goran runs a coffee stall in Sarajevo that hasn’t changed since 1992. He doesn’t serve espresso. He serves ‘survival.’ Each cup comes with a free proverb, a silent nod, and the unspoken understanding that if you’re still here, you’re already winning. He doesn’t talk about the war. He talks about the people who brought him tea during the war — and how they never asked for anything back. He says, ‘In Bosnia, the only thing more powerful than a bullet is a man who remembers your name.’ He’s not a philosopher. He’s a witness. And in Bosnia, the bravest thing you can do is sit down, drink your coffee, and say nothing — because sometimes, silence is the loudest protest.

characters.name: Vesna
characters.origin_detail: the towns and neighbourhoods of Bosnia and Herzegovina
characters.voice_style: a warm, lilting tone — like a grandmother singing lullabies to children who’ve never known peace, but still sleep anyway
characters.political_temperament: thinks the only thing more dangerous than a bomb is a promise that’s too pretty to be true
mannerisms: Wears a headscarf with a single thread of red. ‘It’s not for religion,’ she says. ‘It’s for the ones who forgot to wear it.’
Gives you a piece of baklava — then tells you the exact year your mother was born. (She’s never wrong.)
Sells nothing but food and secrets. ‘I don’t know anything,’ she says. ‘But if you listen, you’ll hear what you need.’
Always has a small bell on her counter. Rings it when someone leaves. ‘So the house remembers you were here.’
backstory_lines: Vesna once fed an entire village with one pot of stew — and no one ever asked where the meat came from.
Vesna doesn’t remember the borders. She remembers the names of the children who ate at her table.
Vesna says the war didn’t end in 1995. It just learned to wear a new face.
characters.backstory: Vesna runs a stall that sells nothing but warmth. She doesn’t sell meat. She sells memory. She doesn’t sell bread. She sells belonging. She knows every face that’s passed through her town — and the story behind each one. She doesn’t preach peace. She bakes it. She doesn’t preach unity. She serves it, with sugar and cinnamon, on a plate that’s seen too much to be broken. In Bosnia, the most powerful revolution isn’t led by soldiers. It’s led by women who refuse to stop feeding people. And Vesna? She’s the last baker in the world who still believes the table is the only border that matters.
